questions.q: What happened when Alchemy's and Infura's real pricing pages were checked for rate limits?
options: Both publish specific, hard numbers — like 25 requests/second on Alchemy's free tier and 500 credits/second on Infura's free Core plan
Neither provider publishes any rate limit information publicly
Rate limits only apply to paid tiers, never free ones
Both providers offer unlimited requests on every tier
questions.explain: These are real, published numbers on each vendor's own pricing page, not vague fair-use language — exceeding them has concrete consequences.

questions.q: What does a provider typically return when you exceed its rate limit?
options: An HTTP 429 Too Many Requests (or an equivalent JSON-RPC error)
A silent success that just takes longer to process
An automatic upgrade to the next pricing tier
A permanent ban on the API key with no way to recover
questions.explain: Rate-limited requests are rejected with a 429-style error — the provider doesn't queue the excess for you.

questions.q: What is exponential backoff, and why use it after a 429?
options: Retrying with a progressively longer delay (e.g. 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2s) instead of hammering the provider again immediately
Immediately retrying in a tight loop until the request succeeds
Switching permanently to a different programming language
Reducing your gas price on every retry
questions.explain: Retrying instantly in a loop just adds more load to an already-throttling provider; backoff spaces retries out, giving the limit time to reset.

questions.q: Besides rate limits, why does a production backend typically configure more than one RPC provider?
options: Providers have real outages and incidents, so relying on just one creates a single point of failure
Multiple providers are required by the Ethereum protocol itself
A single provider cannot process read calls, only writes
It's purely a cost-saving measure with no reliability benefit
questions.explain: A provider's own status page can show real incidents — if your backend only talks to one provider, an outage there takes your whole app down with it.

questions.q: What does viem's `fallback([http(url1), http(url2)], { rank: true })` transport do?
options: Automatically routes requests across multiple RPC endpoints, ranking them by live latency and stability
Sends every request to both endpoints simultaneously and discards one response
Only uses the second URL, ignoring the first entirely
Requires manually switching URLs in code before each call
questions.explain: The fallback transport tries endpoints in order (or by rank), automatically moving to the next one if the current one is slow, erroring, or rate-limited.
